title: Keeping ChatGPT Fast as AI Development Accelerates
gist: Martin Spier, who leads ChatGPT performance at OpenAI, describes two simultaneous accelerations — user growth (900 million weekly actives as of February, roughly 11% of humanity) and agentic-coding change velocity (PR volume per engineer up 70% by October 2025, before the latest coding-agent wave) — and argues the resulting compounding latency and resource drag is mostly NOT in GPUs but in the CPU, I/O, data-fetch and tokenization path around inference. His answer is to industrialize performance engineering with always-on agents running reactive (regression to profile to fix to verify) and active (continuous optimization search) loops, which only works if test coverage, benchmarks, observability, written architecture context and safe-rollout machinery already exist.

insights.claim: Two accelerations are compounding simultaneously for consumer software: companies reach their first millions of users far faster than before, and agentic coding is raising the rate at which change enters production systems.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Load growth and change growth stack multiplicatively on the same infrastructure, so capacity planning built on one of the two curves will be wrong.
insights.locator: Today I want to tell you guys a story about two accelerations

insights.claim: The long-standing assumption that a human understood every change going into production is no longer true, because engineers delegate to agents at a higher abstraction layer and do not know the details of everything shipping.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Loss of human comprehension per change is a new class of operational risk that automated detection, not review headcount, has to absorb.
insights.quote: the abstraction layer is a bit higher
insights.locator: The third thing is, previously, we always had this assumption

insights.claim: The surge in agentic change volume is straining not only performance but the surrounding developer infrastructure — code hosting, CI engines and repositories — because far more changes must be processed per engineer.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Agentic coding creates a secondary demand shock for CI/CD and code-hosting capacity, a monetizable tailwind for those vendors.
insights.locator: Anyone from GitHub, GitLab here

insights.claim: ChatGPT was launched in late 2022 as a research preview, not as a consumer application designed for hundreds of millions of users, and only acquired latency, reliability and support requirements once users arrived.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: The architecture carries research-preview origins, which explains why so much performance work is retrofit rather than design.
insights.locator: Going into ChatGPT, a bit of the history

insights.claim: ChatGPT reached its first million users five days after launching as a research preview, a growth onset almost no company can match.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Time-to-first-million is collapsing across the industry, so infrastructure readiness has to precede product-market fit, not follow it.
insights.quote: I think very few companies can tell that they reached their first million users in five days from launch in a research preview.
insights.locator: The growth was quite impressive

insights.claim: The last official figure the OpenAI performance lead can share is 900 million weekly active users of ChatGPT as of February, roughly 11% of the human population.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: A concrete, first-party denominator for sizing ChatGPT's inference and non-inference compute demand and monetization runway.
insights.quote: That's 900 million people using ChatGPT every week. Just to let it sink in, that's almost 11% of the whole human population.
insights.locator: The last official number I can share is from February

insights.claim: ChatGPT growth was not a smooth ramp but spike-driven by viral product launches, with image generation producing over 700 million images from over 130 million users in its first seven days.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Demand arrives as unpredictable step-functions, so headroom, not average utilization, is the binding constraint on AI consumer infrastructure.
insights.quote: Within just the seven first days, over 700 million images were generated by over 130 million users.
insights.locator: you might remember the image generation spike from last year

insights.claim: Serving a global user base forces hard architectural questions about POP placement, application server and GPU locality, regional capacity, inter-datacenter network connectivity, and where data lives and is replicated under local constraints.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Geographic GPU and data placement is an under-modeled cost and latency driver in AI services, distinct from raw accelerator supply.
insights.locator: Chat is not used only in the U.S.

insights.claim: The product changed continuously alongside growth — GPTs, voice, agents, image generation and other launches over less than four years — adding new workloads and more complex supporting architecture.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Workload heterogeneity, not just volume, is what makes AI-product capacity planning hard and drives overprovisioning.
insights.locator: There was a lot of change beyond all just the model changes

insights.claim: OpenAI's shipping rate changed dramatically after the launch of Codex, with the volume of change entering its systems increasing sharply independent of whether that change carries proportional value.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Coding agents are validated as a throughput step-change at the company that builds them, which is the strongest available evidence for the category.
insights.locator: Especially since the launch of Codex, our shipping rate changed dramatically

insights.claim: The surprising effect of capable coding agents is not faster single tasks but developers going multi-threaded, working on seven to ten things at once and unblocking agents as they ping for input.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Parallelism per engineer, not latency per task, is where agentic coding productivity actually shows up — and it is what floods downstream systems.
insights.locator: Developers started going multi-threaded

insights.claim: A DX benchmark puts merged PRs at p90 near five per engineer per week at smaller tech companies, and OpenAI ships considerably faster than that.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: An external yardstick for benchmarking engineering throughput claims when evaluating AI-native software organizations.
insights.quote: At p90, you're almost at five PRs a week per engineer, which is quite fast. We are a lot faster than that.
insights.locator: Some of you might be familiar with this benchmark from DX

insights.claim: By October 2025 — before the most recent wave of coding-agent improvement — the weekly PR volume shipped per OpenAI engineer had already increased by 70%.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: A rare hard number on agentic-coding productivity gains, and explicitly a lagging one — the current figure is presumably higher.
insights.quote: the volume of PRs that our engineers are shipping every week increased by 70%
insights.locator: Even back then, back in October '25

insights.claim: Almost every engineer at OpenAI uses Codex weekly or daily, and every single pull request is automatically reviewed by Codex.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Universal internal adoption including automated review is the deployment pattern enterprises will be sold; it also means review capacity scales with agents, not headcount.
insights.quote: Every single PR gets automatically reviewed by Codex.
insights.locator: Almost every engineer at the company today is using Codex

insights.claim: Codex functions as a general workbench rather than a coding tool: production troubleshooting, querying observability tools to explain metric regressions, data science and analysis, Slack thread summarization, one-on-one prep, document writing and presentation building.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: The agent's addressable surface is all knowledge work in an engineering org, which is a far larger seat-expansion story than code completion.
insights.locator: Codex became the workbench to do everything

insights.claim: Every shipped change — an extra conditional, an extra network request, a data structure held in memory — draws from a shared latency and hardware budget, and the cost is often invisible at first.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: A shared-budget model reframes performance as a balance sheet that agentic shipping draws down faster, requiring proportionally faster paydown.
insights.locator: Shipping all those things, every new feature, every new line of code

insights.claim: The danger is not the visible deploy-to-deploy regression but the accumulation of individually undetectable small changes that compound until headroom or latency becomes a problem.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Detection tooling tuned to step-change regressions will miss the dominant failure mode; drift metrics are the gap to fill.
insights.locator: I'm not talking purely about those big regressions

insights.claim: Cloud elasticity is a myth at this scale — memory and RAM are finite and the cloud cannot expand forever, so inefficiency directly consumes a hard resource ceiling.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: At hyperscale AI volumes, software efficiency becomes a capacity strategy, not a cost-optimization nicety.
insights.quote: Everyone will raise, cloud can expand forever. No, it cannot.
insights.locator: Same goes for hardware resources

insights.claim: Accumulated performance debt surfaces in three distinct ways: user-visible slowness, paying more to run the identical workload, and shrinking headroom for growth.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Ties performance work directly to gross margin and to capacity runway, which is how to justify it in an AI cost structure.
insights.locator: That damage from all those small changes

insights.claim: A scalability problem eventually becomes a reliability problem, at the point where the system can no longer absorb a spike or grow.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Headroom erosion is a leading indicator of outages, so track spare capacity as a reliability metric rather than a cost metric.
insights.quote: a scalability problem will become a reliability problem at some point when you cannot absorb that spike anymore, when you cannot grow anymore
insights.locator: For scalability, you have less and less headroom to grow

insights.claim: Feature shipping and performance engineering are two opposing forces held in balance, and agentic coding sped up only one side of that equation, breaking the balance.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Any org adopting coding agents without scaling its counterbalancing quality/perf loop is accumulating unmeasured debt.
insights.locator: In one side, you have people shipping features

insights.claim: Hiring more performance engineers is explicitly rejected as the answer because perf engineers are hard to find, so the workflow itself must be accelerated instead.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Scarce specialist labor is what forces automation of specialist workflows — the same logic will hit SRE, security and QA functions.
insights.locator: The answer to that is, of course, we don't want to hire more performance engineers

insights.claim: Performance measurably affects user retention and acquisition, a correlation the speaker modeled at both Netflix and OpenAI: slowness and errors show up as users canceling plans.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Latency is a revenue variable with a modelable elasticity, which makes performance spending defensible against product spending.
insights.locator: Performance affects user retention and acquisition

insights.claim: Adding review friction such as requiring five humans to review every AI-generated PR would destroy the throughput advantage agents provide, so the fix has to come from faster perf loops rather than added gates.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Governance-by-human-gate is economically self-defeating in agentic orgs; the market for automated verification is the consequence.
insights.locator: Every AI PR that is open needs to be reviewed by five humans

themes.theme: Measuring perceived latency, not inference metrics

insights.claim: AI teams over-index on inference component metrics such as time to first token, tokens per second and throughput, but inference is only a chunk of the user journey rather than the whole problem.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Vendors and buyers benchmarking on TTFT alone are optimizing a partial metric; end-to-end journey latency is the differentiator.
insights.locator: everyone is very focused on inference

insights.claim: The right latency model tracks a user's action journey in stages: immediate acknowledgment on submit, then first visible value when the user can start reading, then stream cadence fast enough not to block reading, then task completion.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: A reusable measurement scheme for any streaming AI product, and the basis for SLOs that actually correlate with churn.
insights.locator: The users have different expectations along the action journey

insights.claim: Deciding where to stop the latency timer is a product judgment, not a technical one: whether completion means thinking tokens or the final message, or a first low-resolution image versus the final generated image.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Cross-vendor latency comparisons are unreliable unless the timer-stop definition is disclosed — a due-diligence question for AI benchmarks.
insights.locator: When you have a thinking response, where do you stop the timer?

insights.claim: User intent must be a measurement dimension because expectations differ sharply: a simple factual question carries search-engine expectations while an agentic loop or image generation is expected to take longer.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Aggregate p50/p99 latency without intent segmentation hides both the failures that lose users and the headroom that is safe to spend.
insights.locator: Having those intents is super important as a dimension

insights.claim: Wall-clock user time should be decomposed into system evidence via a latency breakdown or layer-cake chart showing client work, networking, data fetching, serialization and tokenization alongside inference.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Without full-path decomposition, teams default to blaming inference and misallocate optimization effort — and GPU spend.
insights.locator: Your latency breakdown chart or layer cake

insights.claim: Before a chat message reaches the inference engine the system must verify user and client identity, check the user's plan, quotas and state, then fetch conversation history, uploaded files such as PDFs and images, and project context.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: The pre-inference path is a data-retrieval problem, which is why storage and database performance are first-order costs in AI products.
insights.locator: There's a lot that happens before a message gets sent to the inference engine

insights.claim: After data assembly the system still performs per-model encoding and tokenization, context-window checks, possible truncation or compaction, assembly for the inference engine, then streaming back and persisting the conversation.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Tokenization and context management are real CPU line items at scale, not free preprocessing — relevant to anyone modeling AI serving cost.
insights.locator: There's encoding. There's tokenization

insights.claim: The user's message is a small ingredient of a data-heavy payload: conversations can be megabytes, tens of megabytes, or possibly hundreds of megabytes long.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Long-conversation data volume drives storage, I/O and egress costs that scale with engagement, not with tokens generated.
insights.quote: You might have conversations that are megabytes long, tens of megabytes long, maybe hundreds of megabytes long.
insights.locator: Especially for long conversations, they are pretty data heavy

insights.claim: Serving ChatGPT consumes heavy traditional non-GPU resources — database requests, blob storage, I/O, CPU for serialization and deserialization, and RAM to hold state.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: AI infrastructure demand is not GPU-only; CPU, storage and networking suppliers get pulled along by consumer AI scale.
insights.locator: when people think about AI, the first thing that comes to mind is GPUs

insights.claim: More code change lands in the non-inference components affecting CPU, memory and I/O than in the inference engine itself, so the bulk of regression risk sits outside the model stack.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Performance tooling investment should follow change volume, which points at application services rather than the model serving layer.
insights.locator: there are shipping rate changes to the actual inference engine

insights.claim: Having the fastest model and the fastest inference engine is irrelevant if the rest of the request path is slow, because the user experiences the whole path and leaves on that basis.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Model-benchmark leadership does not convert into product speed, which limits the competitive value of raw model latency wins.
insights.quote: It doesn't matter that I have an extremely fast model, the fastest model, the fastest inference engine, if the rest of the path is slow.
insights.locator: Why is that important?

insights.claim: The classic reactive performance loop — spot a regression, capture CPU profiles, compare before and after, map code changes to stacks, design and implement an optimization, ship and test — is serial, human-bound and too slow for agentic shipping rates.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: The bottleneck is loop latency, not analyst skill, which is precisely the shape of problem agents can attack.
insights.locator: Usually, our reactive loop, it takes quite a bit of time

insights.claim: OpenAI already has performance skills in Codex that fire profiles and compare two profiles automatically, with the agent using codebase access to identify which PRs entered the window and propose a fix.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Automated profile-diff-to-fix is shipped capability today, not aspiration — a concrete benchmark for observability vendors' agent roadmaps.
insights.locator: We have performance skills on Codex to do that

insights.claim: Slow drift can be caught with fine-grained proxy metrics such as code complexity or the number of network requests executed during a benchmark, enabling agents to act on regressions too small to see in aggregate telemetry.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Proxy drift metrics are the practical instrumentation gap most teams have not built, and the precondition for catching compounding debt.
insights.locator: Same goes for drift. Small regressions

insights.claim: Pre-production CI can catch the boring performance issues, but many performance problems only manifest in production under specific combinations of user workloads and cannot be caught before merge at all.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Shift-left performance testing has a hard ceiling; production profiling and safe automated remediation are the necessary complement.
insights.locator: there's a lot of things, especially on the perf side, that don't manifest until they get to production

insights.claim: The automatable pre-production surface includes microbenchmarks on every PR (which agents can also write), method-level regression monitoring on the latency critical path, memory allocation profiling, and bundle-size budgets for mobile.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist of agent-automatable perf gates that any engineering org can adopt without OpenAI-scale infrastructure.
insights.locator: We can have microbenchmarks running all the time on every single PR

insights.claim: Many agent-proposed fixes will simply not work, and the correct posture is to discard them and fire multiple parallel threads with multiple ideas rather than serialize on one hypothesis.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Agent value comes from cheap parallel failure, so cost models must budget for discarded work rather than assume high hit rates.
insights.locator: Yes, many times that fix will not work

insights.claim: Teams unwilling to let an agent deploy to production unsupervised can still get almost all the way there by having the agent submit a PR that implements a performance-optimization experiment.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: A pragmatic adoption ladder: most of the automation benefit is available without granting agents production write access.
insights.locator: If you're not at a stage where you can fully trust an agent to deploy to production

insights.claim: The most promising direction is translating individual performance engineers' niche skill sets into always-on agent skills that continuously scan code, traces and logs for optimizations — to the point that engineers name agents after the specialists they encode and start treating them as people.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Encoding scarce expert skill into reusable agent skills is the mechanism by which specialist labor scarcity stops constraining output.
insights.quote: I have a Ben agent. I have a Brendan agent. I have lots of agents named as people. Then you start treating them as people at some point too.
insights.locator: The always-on loop is the one that probably excites me the most

insights.claim: Autonomy scales only when agents can complete a full loop — trigger, idea, implementation, and measurement of whether the change actually helped — without human intervention at any step.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Closing the loop, not raw model capability, is what removes the human bottleneck — the design criterion for evaluating agent platforms.
insights.locator: When you can get agents to complete full loops

insights.claim: Engineering maturity becomes more valuable in the agentic era, not less: good test coverage, benchmarks, explicit contracts between system components, broad observability, and safe rollout with automated canary analysis or blue-green pushes.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Organizations with weak testing and observability cannot safely capture agentic productivity, which widens the gap between mature and immature engineering orgs.
insights.locator: Your engineering maturity becomes more important

insights.claim: Observability blind spots are dangerous with agents because, unlike humans, an agent has no intuition about the system and will likely go in the wrong direction when coverage is missing.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Agent adoption creates a hard requirement for observability coverage, a durable demand driver for telemetry vendors.
insights.locator: If there's blind spots, it's very likely that it might go in the wrong direction

insights.claim: Performance optimization is fundamentally a search problem, which is why agents that can try alternatives and compare benchmarks in parallel change its economics.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Any engineering task reducible to search-with-a-clear-signal is a candidate for the same agent treatment — a screen for where automation lands next.
insights.quote: At the end of the day, all those perf optimizations, that's a search problem.
insights.locator: At the end of the day, all those perf optimizations

insights.claim: Feedback loop speed determines whether agents add value at all: a twelve-hour loop leaves little advantage over human interruption, while minutes-scale feedback lets agents keep moving.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Investment in fast benchmark and test infrastructure is the gating factor for agent ROI, ahead of model quality.
insights.quote: If your feedback loop might be 12 hours, then maybe your agent doesn't really add that much value
insights.locator: Fast feedback is important too

insights.claim: A wrong metric is worse than no metric under automation, because the agent will faithfully optimize the wrong thing and the product does not actually improve.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Metric definition becomes a high-leverage governance task once optimization is automated and runs continuously.
insights.quote: If I'm measuring the wrong thing, the agent will optimize the wrong thing and I'm not actually improving the product in the first place.
insights.locator: That measurement you have, it just guides the agent

insights.claim: Reproducing production workloads reliably is a prerequisite for agent-driven optimization, otherwise the agent optimizes against a benchmark that does not match production.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Workload fidelity is the quiet dependency that decides whether automated optimization compounds or drifts into waste.
insights.locator: If you're actually trying to reproduce a production workload

insights.claim: Agents lack tribal knowledge, so written architecture definitions, deploy details, observability data and codebase context must be supplied explicitly — while still managing what fits in the context window.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Documentation stops being optional overhead and becomes machine-readable input that determines agent output quality.
insights.quote: Different than humans, you don't have tribal knowledge here.
insights.locator: If you have actual written down definitions of the architecture

insights.claim: The target end state is humans setting direction while agents do the work — specifically the boring work that does not involve deciding what is good or bad.
insights.speaker: Martin Spier
insights.so_what: Judgment and direction-setting are the retained human functions in this model, which shapes where engineering headcount value concentrates.
insights.quote: we are working towards a world where humans are just setting the direction and our agents are just doing all the work
insights.locator: General idea, we are working towards a world
